hero.title: Blockchain Fundamentals: blocks, hashing and consensus
hero.subtitle: Hash text live, tamper with a chain, edit a Merkle tree, calculate mining time and attack odds in a spreadsheet, and design a consensus rulebook. Every task is checked and explained.
hero.outcomeLine: After this course you can explain and critique how blockchains agree on a shared history.

faq.a: No. The labs run in your browser and the maths uses a spreadsheet.

faq.q: Is this enough to build a blockchain?
faq.a: It gives you the concepts. The Ethereum and Solidity courses in this series go on to building.
They are simplified teaching models. Real networks use more detailed target arithmetic, and the course says where it simplifies.

activities.title: How many transactions per second?
activities.objective: Work out transaction throughput from block size, transaction size and block time, and compare chains.
activities.scenario: Throughput is limited by how much data fits in a block and how often blocks arrive. The numbers below are teaching figures, not live data.
steps: In D2 work out how many transactions fit in a block: block size in bytes divided by average transaction size, rounded down with INT.
In E2 work out transactions per second: D2 divided by block time in seconds.
In F2 work out transactions per day: E2 times 86400.
Fill down rows 2 to 4.
In B8 find the highest throughput with MAX.

checks.label: D2 is transactions per block for chain A
checks.explain: Divide block size by transaction size and round down.

checks.label: E2 is chain A's transactions per second
checks.explain: Divide by the block time in seconds.

checks.label: F3 is chain B's transactions per day
E4 is chain C's transactions per second
B8 is the highest throughput

activities.title: How big is a Merkle tree?
activities.objective: Count hashes in a Merkle tree and see how short a proof is.
activities.scenario: In a Merkle tree with n leaves (a power of two), a proof that one transaction is included needs one hash per level, and the number of levels above the leaves is how many times you can halve n before reaching 1.
steps: The number of transactions (leaves) in column B is given.
In C2 to C6 type the proof length: the number of levels above the leaves, which is how many times you can halve the leaves before reaching 1: 2, 3, 4, 10 and 20.
In D2 work out the total hashes in the tree: 2 times the leaves minus 1. Fill down.
In E2 work out how much smaller the proof is than the leaves: leaves divided by proof length. Fill down.

checks.label: C2 is 2
checks.explain: Four leaves have two levels above them.

checks.label: C6 is 20
D2 is the total hashes
checks.explain: A full binary tree has 2n minus 1 nodes.

checks.label: D6 fills down
E6 is leaves per proof hash
checks.explain: A huge block needs only 20 hashes to prove one transaction.

activities.title: How long does mining take?
activities.objective: Estimate expected tries and time to find a block from the difficulty and the miner's hash rate.
activities.scenario: A valid hash must start with a number of zero bits. Each extra zero bit doubles the expected number of tries. A miner tries a fixed number of hashes per second. (Teaching model, simpler than Bitcoin's real target arithmetic.)
steps: In B6 work out expected tries: 2 raised to the number of leading zero bits (B2) using POWER.
In B7 work out the seconds a single miner needs on average: expected tries divided by hash rate (B3).
In B8 convert to minutes: B7 divided by 60.
In B9 work out the seconds if 1,000 identical miners share the work: B7 divided by 1000.
In B10 show the number of extra zero bits needed to make it 16 times harder: leave B2 plus 4, as a number.

checks.label: B6 is the expected tries
checks.explain: Each extra bit doubles the work.

checks.label: B7 is the seconds for one miner
checks.explain: Tries divided by hashes per second.

checks.label: B8 is the minutes
B9 is the time for 1,000 miners
checks.explain: Work shared among many miners finishes sooner.

checks.label: B10 is the bits for 16 times harder
checks.explain: Four extra bits multiply the work by 2^4 = 16.

cells.A3: Hash rate of one miner (hashes per second)

activities.title: Can an attacker catch up?
activities.objective: Use the simple catch-up probability to see why more confirmations are safer.
activities.scenario: If an attacker controls a fraction q of the hash power and the honest network controls p = 1 − q, the chance that the attacker ever catches up from z blocks behind is (q ÷ p) raised to the power z, when q is smaller than p (a standard simplified result).
steps: In B3 work out p, the honest share: 1 minus q (B2).
In B4 work out the ratio q divided by p.
In D2 to D8 work out the catch-up chance for each number of confirmations: POWER of the ratio (B4) to the confirmations in column C.
In B10 show the smallest number of confirmations from the list whose chance is below 0.1%: write it as a number using COUNTIF(D2:D8,">0.001")+1.

checks.label: B3 is the honest share
B4 is q/p
D2 is the chance with 1 confirmation
D8 is the chance with 12 confirmations
B10 is the confirmations needed
checks.explain: Count the rows above the threshold and add one.

activities.title: What does a validator earn?
activities.objective: Calculate staking rewards and the cost of a slashing penalty.
activities.scenario: A validator stakes coins and earns a yearly reward rate. A serious fault slashes a fraction of the stake. (Teaching numbers.)
steps: In B6 work out the yearly reward: stake times the reward rate.
In B7 work out the reward after the validator's commission to a delegator: reward times 1 minus commission.
In B8 work out the loss if slashed: stake times the slash fraction.
In B9 work out how many years of rewards it takes to earn back one slashing event: loss divided by yearly reward.
In B10 show Worth the risk if payback is under 2 years, otherwise Risky.
